faq.title: Can an attacker read my WhatsApp or Signal messages via SS7 hijacking?
faq.description: No. Modern messaging apps like Signal and WhatsApp utilize end-to-end encryption (the Signal Protocol). Private encryption keys are generated and stored exclusively on your physical phone hardware. While an attacker who hijacks your SMS via SS7 could re-register your phone number on a new device, they cannot read your historical message archives.

faq.title: How do hackers get access to the global SS7 signaling network?
faq.description: Historically, only national state carriers had SS7 access. Today, thousands of virtual network operators (MVNOs), SMS marketing aggregators, and small telecom providers in loosely regulated countries have legitimate SS7 global interconnects. Hackers rent access to these commercial gateways on dark web marketplaces or bribe insider telecom operators.

faq.title: Does switching to eSIM protect against SIM swap fraud?
faq.description: No. eSIM protects against physical theft of a plastic SIM card from your device, but SIM swap fraud occurs at the telecom carrier's database level (HLR/HSS). An attacker can convince customer support to generate a fraudulent eSIM QR code just as easily as activating a blank plastic SIM card.

html:
Modern cybersecurity emphasizes end-to-end encryption, cryptographic hardware enclaves, and biometric authentication. Yet millions of bank accounts, corporate databases, and high-profile social media accounts are compromised every year without malware ever touching the victim's smartphone. The Achilles' heel of mobile digital identity does not lie inside your phone's operating system; it resides in the antiquated, trust-based signaling architecture of global telecommunications networks: Signaling System No. 7 (SS7) and its 4G evolution, Diameter.

When an attacker executes a telecom network hijack or SIM swap attack, they exploit protocol-level vulnerabilities dating back to the late 1970s. By manipulating global signaling routing directories, state-sponsored intelligence agencies and sophisticated criminal syndicates can intercept SMS two-factor authentication (2FA) passcodes in real time, eavesdrop on cellular phone calls, and track physical real-world GPS coordinates anywhere on Earth—completely invisible to the victim.

The Evolution of Telecom Signaling: From In-Band to SS7

In the early days of telephony, control signaling (routing commands, call termination, billing pulses) was transmitted over the same physical wire as the human voice. This in-band signaling allowed phone phreaks in the 1960s (including Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak with their famous "Blue Box") to generate a 2600 Hz tone that tricked telephone switches into granting free international trunk lines.

To eliminate in-band exploitation, telecom standards bodies developed Common Channel Signaling (CCS), establishing Signaling System No. 7 (SS7) in 1980. SS7 physically and logically separated call audio channels from network control signaling. Control messages—such as call setup, SMS delivery, roaming handshakes, and subscriber location lookup—were routed over an isolated global signaling data backbone managed by national state telecom monopolies.

Crucially, SS7 was engineered with zero cryptographic authentication. In the 1980s, only a handful of state-regulated postal, telegraph, and telecom (PTT) operators had access to the SS7 signaling network. Every switch within the SS7 network assumed that every message received from any other switch was authentic and trustworthy. That foundational assumption of implicit trust is now the single greatest structural vulnerability in modern digital communications.

SS7 Core Protocol Architecture and MAP Exploitation

SS7 is structured as a four-level protocol stack corresponding roughly to the OSI model:

  • Message Transfer Part (MTP 1–3): Physical, data link, and network routing layers that route signaling packets between Signaling End Points (SEPs) using Signaling Transfer Points (STPs).
  • Signaling Connection Control Part (SCCP): Provides logical routing and global title translation (GTT), analogous to IP routing.
  • Transaction Capabilities Application Part (TCAP): Manages non-circuit-related queries between database registers.
  • Mobile Application Part (MAP): The critical mobile service layer that enables international roaming, SMS delivery, and subscriber location registers.

Mobile networks track devices using two central databases: the Home Location Register (HLR) (the central database containing authorized subscriber profiles and their current serving network) and the Visitor Location Register (VLR) (a local database at the foreign serving network managing active roaming subscribers). Attackers exploit MAP commands to hijack these records:

1. Location Tracking via SendRoutingInfoForSM (SRI-SM)

To deliver an SMS text message to your phone, the sender's network must discover where your phone is physically located. The sender's SMS Center (SMSC) queries your home network's HLR using an SS7 MAP_SEND_ROUTING_INFO_FOR_SM request containing your phone number (MSISDN). Because SS7 lacks authentication, an attacker with rented SS7 gateway access sends an SRI-SM query to your carrier. The carrier's HLR dutifully replies with your phone's unique international identity (IMSI) and the global address of the cellular tower (MSC/VLR Cell ID) your phone is currently connected to—revealing your physical latitude and longitude within meters!

2. SMS 2FA Interception via UpdateLocation Spoofing

Even more devastating is the MAP_UPDATE_LOCATION exploit. When you fly to another country, your phone connects to a local cell tower, prompting the foreign VLR to send an UpdateLocation message to your home HLR, notifying it to reroute your incoming calls and SMS messages to the foreign network. An attacker simulates this exact roaming handshake by injecting a fraudulent UpdateLocation request into the global SS7 network, pointing your phone number to an attacker-controlled virtual VLR switch in another country. Your home carrier redirects all incoming SMS traffic to the attacker's switch. The attacker requests a bank password reset, intercepts the incoming 2FA verification SMS code, and drains your account—while your actual physical phone simply displays "No Service"!

The 4G Diameter Protocol: New Format, Same Vulnerabilities

When the 3GPP consortium designed the 4G LTE architecture, they replaced SS7's binary signaling protocols with Diameter, an IP-based protocol derived from RADIUS that utilizes SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol) transport. Diameter governs LTE subscriber mobility, policy charging, and authentication queries between the MME (Mobility Management Entity) and the HSS (Home Subscriber Server).

While Diameter incorporates optional IPSec and TLS encryption, it inherited the identical structural trust model: carriers assume that Diameter messages originating from international roaming partners are authentic! Furthermore, because 4G networks must maintain backwards compatibility with 2G/3G networks, Diameter-to-SS7 Interworking Function (IWF) gateways bridge both protocols, allowing attackers to tunnel legacy SS7 attack vectors directly into modern LTE core networks.

SIM Swap Fraud: Social Engineering the Core Register

While SS7/Diameter attacks require specialized signaling gateway access (often leased on dark web forums or through corrupt third-party telecom aggregators in weakly regulated jurisdictions), SIM Swap Fraud achieves the identical outcome through physical-layer social engineering:

  1. The attacker collects basic personal information about the target (name, address, date of birth, mother's maiden name) through public data breaches or phishing.
  2. The attacker impersonates the victim, contacting customer care or walking into a retail mobile store, claiming their phone was lost or damaged.
  3. A compromised or duped telecom retail employee enters the victim's phone number into the carrier's internal billing system and assigns it to a blank SIM card held in the attacker's hand.
  4. The carrier's HLR/HSS automatically revokes the cryptographic keys on the legitimate owner's SIM card and activates the attacker's SIM, instantaneously transferring all mobile connectivity, phone calls, and SMS authentication tokens to the adversary.

5G Standalone (5G SA) Defenses: SEPP and Zero-Trust Architecture

To permanently eradicate SS7 and Diameter signaling vulnerabilities, 3GPP engineered the 5G Standalone (5G SA) Core from the ground up using a cloud-native Service-Based Architecture (SBA):

  • HTTP/2 and TLS 1.3: All signaling communication between 5G network functions (AMF, SMF, UDM, AUSF) utilizes modern RESTful JSON APIs running over mutual TLS (mTLS) encrypted HTTP/2 transport.
  • OAuth 2.0 Token Authorization: Network functions cannot communicate simply because they reside on the internal network; every API query requires cryptographic OAuth 2.0 token validation issued by a Network Repository Function (NRF).
  • Security Edge Protection Proxy (SEPP): When roaming between different international carriers, all signaling must traverse a hardened SEPP firewall. The SEPP provides end-to-end cryptographic integrity, message filtering, and PRAS (Public Key Infrastructure) validation over the inter-carrier N32 interface, permanently blocking unauthenticated location queries and routing hijack attempts.
  • SUPI / SUCI Encryption: In 5G networks, your phone's permanent subscriber identity (SUPI) is never broadcast over the air. The smartphone's 5G SIM encrypts the SUPI using the carrier's public cryptographic key, generating an ephemeral Subscription Concealed Identifier (SUCI) that changes with every connection, preventing IMSI-catchers (Stingrays) from tracking users.

How Users Must Protect Themselves from Telecom Hijacking

Because SS7 and SIM swap attacks bypass phone-level operating system controls, users must systematically decouple their security from SMS and cellular phone numbers:

  1. Eradicate SMS-Based 2FA: Immediately replace SMS authentication with hardware FIDO2/WebAuthn security keys (YubiKeys) or time-based one-time password (TOTP) authenticator apps (Aegis, Ente Auth, Google Authenticator). Hardware security keys are mathematically immune to SIM swap and SS7 attacks because cryptographic handshakes occur locally with the browser.
  2. Enable Carrier SIM Lock / PIN: Contact your cellular provider and set up a strict Account Verbal PIN / Port-Out Freeze. Mandate that SIM re-assignments require in-person government photo ID verification at a corporate retail store.
  3. Switch to Encrypted VoIP for Sensitive Services: Where SMS cannot be disabled (such as certain banking apps), register a secondary, unlisted Google Voice or private VoIP number that is secured behind a hardware-keyed Google account rather than tied to your physical SIM card.

CAMEL and Global Title Translation (GTT) Manipulation

To orchestrate sophisticated billing and prepaid roaming intelligence, SS7 networks implement CAMEL (Customised Applications for Mobile networks Enhanced Logic). CAMEL allows home network operators to monitor active calls and inject routing instructions into foreign switches.

In an advanced state-sponsored attack vector known as CAMEL Fraud Hijacking, an adversary injects a MAP_ANY_TIME_INTERROGATION (ATI) or ProvideSubscriberInfo (PSI) message into the signaling mesh. By manipulating Global Title Translation (GTT)—the routing directory that resolves carrier network addresses—the attacker tricks foreign telecommunications switches into routing call audio through an intermediary interception bridge (Man-in-the-Middle) before relaying it to the real recipient. The call connects normally without delay or audible clicks, allowing attackers to record voice conversations and capture dual-tone multi-frequency (DTMF) banking touch-tones in real time.

Mobile Network Operator (MNO) Signaling Firewalls

To defend against external signaling abuse, leading telecommunications carriers deploy high-throughput SS7 and Diameter Signaling Firewalls at international gateway exchanges. These firewalls implement deep packet inspection (DPI) to enforce strict heuristic validation rules:

  1. Velocity Checks: If an UpdateLocation request originates from a foreign network in London just 5 minutes after the subscriber made a phone call in Tokyo, the firewall immediately flags and drops the packet as physically impossible travel.
  2. Origin Filtering: SRI-SM queries arriving from non-whitelisted foreign virtual operators or suspicious SMS aggregators are blocked or answered with randomized dummy data.
  3. CAT / STIR/SHAKEN Cryptographic Attestation: Under modern VoIP standards, caller ID spoofing is mitigated by digital certificate signing (STIR/SHAKEN), ensuring that the originating carrier cryptographically certifies the caller's authorized phone number.
